On Monday morning the class buzzed about Saturday's birthday outing. Karthik listened from his desk. Nobody had said his name, and nobody had said “not you” either. That was the thing. Sunaina posted a group photo, the whole row of friends squeezed together, twelve people tagged. Karthik scrolled through the tags twice. His name wasn't there, and it hadn't been last time either.

At lunch he sat at the end of the bench and nobody moved over. When they stood up to leave, nobody looked back to see if he was coming. Walking to the bus he replayed everything he had said that week. Maybe he was too quiet. Maybe his jokes were boring. Maybe something about him was just wrong.

qa.q: How many people were tagged in Sunaina's group photo?
qa.a: Twelve people were tagged in Sunaina's group photo.

qa.q: How was Karthik feeling on the walk to the bus?
qa.a: Karthik felt hurt and left out, and began doubting himself, replaying everything he had said that week and wondering whether something was wrong with him.

qa.q: What small step could help Karthik that does not depend on that group?
qa.a: Karthik could ask one person in class for a small plan, join an activity built on a shared interest, or tell a trusted adult about feeling left out.

qa.q: How might Sunaina see the photo and the tags?
qa.a: Sunaina probably thought of it as an ordinary post about a fun day and did not think about who was missing.

grounding: A teenager is not openly bullied but is never invited, tagged or waited for, and gradually starts to think something is wrong with them.

“You're home early,” Jomon bhaiya said, looking up from his laptop. “No cricket?”

“Nobody waited for me at the gate,” Lalit said, dropping the bag. “They all left.”

“Maybe they forgot.”

“They always forget.” Lalit stared at the floor. “I'm not in the group chat, you know. Not since Class 8.”

“Since the group started?”

“No idea. I just never got the message.” Lalit's voice went small. “Maybe I'm boring.”

Jomon shut the laptop. “You're not boring. Last night you made Amma laugh so hard she spilled the tea.”

“That doesn't count. Amma has to laugh.”

“Okay, then come to my practice on Saturday. My friends like new faces.”

Lalit shrugged, but did not say no.

qa.q: Since which class has Lalit not been in the group chat?
qa.a: Lalit has not been in the group chat since Class 8.

qa.q: What does Lalit mean by saying, “Maybe I'm boring”?
qa.a: Lalit feels ignored and is starting to believe something is wrong with Lalit personally.

qa.q: What did Jomon offer Lalit as a next step?
qa.a: Jomon invited Lalit to come to practice on Saturday, where friends like new faces.

qa.q: How might Jomon have felt hearing that nobody waited for Lalit at the gate?
qa.a: Jomon probably felt concerned and protective, choosing gentle words and a practical invitation.

grounding: A teenager is never invited, tagged or waited for, and being ignored gradually convinces them something is wrong with them personally.

passage:
I'm Anirban, and Class 9 was the year I became invisible.
Nobody bullied me. That's the strange part. No one was mean. I just wasn't invited. Birthday photos appeared online, and I wasn't in them. Group projects formed before I even looked up. When the class went for ice cream after the exam, they'd already left by the time I packed my bag. Nobody waited.
After a few months, I started thinking there must be something wrong with me. My voice, my face, my jokes. I stopped talking in class.
Then, in Class 10, Kavitha asked me to be in her science group. Just like that. I remember how shocked I was. I remember thinking, oh. Maybe it wasn't me.

qa.q: Who asked Anirban to join a science group in Class 10?
qa.a: Kavitha did.

qa.q: How did Anirban feel after months of not being invited?
qa.a: Anirban felt invisible and began to feel ashamed, thinking something was wrong with Anirban's voice, face or jokes.

qa.q: What does Kavitha's invitation show about how to help someone left out?
qa.a: A simple, ordinary invitation can break the pattern and show the person they are not the problem.

qa.q: How might the class have seen Anirban that year?
qa.a: They probably didn't notice much; it wasn't meanness, just not thinking to include the quiet one.

grounding: A teenager recalls being quietly left out, never invited or waited for, until the exclusion brought the belief that something was wrong with the writer.

passage:
School counsellor's note, Class 10, Thursday.
Ganga came to see me today, very quietly. She is not being bullied, she said. “Nobody does anything to me. That's the problem. I'm just not there for them.”
She described the class group chat where plans are made she's never tagged in, a birthday picnic she saw only in photos, and the walk to the bus stop where her old friend Keerthana now walks ahead with others.
Then she asked, “Is something wrong with me? Maybe I'm boring.”
I told her clearly that being left out does not mean something is wrong with her. We talked about one club she might join. I'll meet her again Monday, and with her permission, I'll speak to her class teacher about mixing groups for projects.

qa.q: Who used to walk with Ganga to the bus stop?
qa.a: Her old friend Keerthana.

qa.q: How was Ganga feeling when she asked if something was wrong with her?
qa.a: She felt hurt and ashamed, starting to believe the quiet exclusion meant she was boring or wrong.

qa.q: What steps did the counsellor take, and why are they helpful?
qa.a: The counsellor told her clearly it wasn't her fault, suggested a club, and planned a follow-up and project mixing, so she isn't left alone with it.

qa.q: How might Keerthana see the walks to the bus stop?
qa.a: Keerthana may not have noticed Ganga being left behind, simply drifting towards a new group.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a teenager who is never invited or waited for, gradually convinced something is wrong with her.

passage:
Saturday night
The party photos are up. Everybody from our class was at Tanya's. Everyone except me and maybe two others. I didn't even know there was a party.
It's not like anyone was mean. That's what makes it worse. Nobody told me not to come. They just didn't think of me.
Even Jeevan, who sits with me in tuition, didn't wait after class on Friday. He just walked off with the others, laughing.
I keep looking in the mirror. Is it my face? Do I talk too much? Too little? There must be something.
Mumma asked why I skipped dinner. I said headache. I don't know how to explain being nobody's first thought.
Sarika

qa.q: Whose party was it?
qa.a: It was at Tanya's.

qa.q: How is Sarika feeling after seeing the photos?
qa.a: Sarika feels hurt, invisible and ashamed, starting to believe something is wrong with Sarika personally.

qa.q: What would help Sarika most right now?
qa.a: Telling Mumma what really happened, and later reaching out to one classmate, could ease the feeling of being alone with it.

qa.q: How might Jeevan have seen Friday after tuition?
qa.a: He probably didn't think about it, just walking off with the group, unaware of how it felt.

grounding: A teenager writes about being quietly left out of plans and photos, slowly convinced something is wrong with them.
